title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: FBI warns attackers are hijacking internet-facing PLCs — the same controllers on your plant floor
items.content_text: A confirmed, active campaign is remotely tampering with internet-facing programmable logic controllers, and the FBI’s warning lands squarely on the plant floor. In a 30 July public service announcement, the FBI and EPA said that since 27 July, water and wastewater utilities in at least seven states reported attackers reaching internet-exposed Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs, changing their IP addresses and passwords to knock out monitoring and control — and in at least one case altering ladder logic across several sites. Reported effects included loss of pressure and flooding. The victims are water utilities, but the FBI stressed the same exposure applies to other branded PLCs — the internet-reachable Rockwell, Siemens and Schneider controllers manufacturers run every day. Any plant with a PLC or cellular modem reachable from the internet should treat this as a direct warning.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Issued 30 Jul 2026 — incidents reported since 27 Jul, ongoing; FBI has not publicly attributed

items.title: Iran-affiliated actors are rewriting plant-floor PLC logic and disabling safety functions
items.content_text: The updated federal advisory AA26-097A (22 July) confirms Iran-affiliated actors reaching internet-exposed PLCs — Rockwell CompactLogix and Micro850, Siemens S7-1200, Schneider Modicon M340 — extracting project files and modifying or deleting control logic, including Add-On Instructions, and manipulating HMI/SCADA displays. In some cases they disabled critical shutdown and alarm logic, letting equipment enter unsafe conditions without operator notification. For manufacturers that is the nightmare case: an engineering workstation or exposed controller becomes a path to silently altered process logic and defeated interlocks.

items.title: Coca-Cola’s Fairlife restarts US production after ransomware halt; data theft confirmed
items.content_text: Coca-Cola’s Fairlife subsidiary has resumed most production at its four US plants after a roughly ten-day shutdown triggered by a 16 July ransomware attack — a reminder that on the plant floor an IT compromise fast becomes an operations problem. In a 27 July update Coca-Cola said most operations were restored and confirmed attackers stole data; the Anubis group claimed the attack and listed the company on its leak site. US facilities were stopped precautionarily while Canadian operations continued. Manufacturing — and food and beverage especially, with just-in-time perishable output — offers attackers exactly the operational leverage that drives a fast payout.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 16 Jul 2026 — updated 27 Jul: production resumed, data theft confirmed

items.title: Manufacturing stays the #1 ransomware target — and attackers now hit the backups first
items.content_text: Manufacturing remains the most-targeted industrial sector for ransomware in 2026, and Sophos’ latest State of Ransomware finds the vast majority of attacks now deliberately target backups — turning the last line of defense into a primary objective and driving recovery costs sharply higher when backups are compromised. Manufacturing’s recovery problem is structural: OT and control-system configurations rarely restore from IT-style backups, so an IT-to-OT ransomware event can idle production lines for weeks. RaaS crews such as Qilin, Akira and SafePay run the same double-extortion playbook — valid credentials, exposed remote access, and data theft before encryption.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Sophos State of Ransomware 2026 / Industrial Cyber

items.title: July ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens ships a CVSS-10 auth-bypass among nine advisories
items.content_text: July’s ICS Patch Tuesday saw Siemens, Schneider Electric and Rockwell publish fixes across their product lines. Siemens alone issued nine advisories including several criticals — a CVSS-10 token-invalidation/authentication-bypass flaw in Opencenter X that grants full application access, plus criticals affecting Mendix, SIMATIC S7-1500, Cadra and Desigo CC. Many stem from third-party components and enable code execution, denial of service, data exposure or privilege escalation. No public exploitation is reported, but the CVSS-10 auth bypass warrants prompt attention on affected deployments.

items.title: Cisco Secure FMC has hard-coded credentials — exploited as a zero-day, now in CISA KEV
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-20316 to its KEV catalog on 29 July after Cisco warned the flaw — hard-coded static credentials for a low-privileged account in the Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) web interface — was exploited as a zero-day. An unauthenticated remote attacker can log in with the built-in credentials and read sensitive data; Cisco rates the impact high because it can be chained with other FMC bugs to escalate. FMC manages the firewalls that often enforce IT/OT segmentation, so a compromised management plane is a direct threat to the boundary protecting the plant floor. Base CVSS is 5.3, but active exploitation makes patching urgent.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 29 Jul 2026 — actively exploited

items.title: Fresh CISA advisory: DoS flaw in Rockwell CompactLogix / ControlLogix comms modules
items.content_text: In its 30 July ICS advisory batch, CISA flagged a vulnerability (ICSA-26-211-05) in Rockwell Automation’s CompactLogix 5380, ControlLogix 5580 and 1756-EN4TR communication modules that a network attacker could use to force a denial-of-service condition, knocking a controller or its EtherNet/IP comms offline. These controllers sit at the heart of discrete and process lines, so an availability bug there translates directly to lost production or a tripped process. No public exploitation is reported; apply Rockwell’s fixes and keep these modules on a segmented, monitored control network.

items.title: Fairlife’s 8-K puts SEC cyber-incident disclosure back on the plant manager’s radar
items.content_text: Coca-Cola’s prompt SEC filing over the Fairlife ransomware attack is a live example of how material cyber incidents at manufacturers now trigger securities-disclosure obligations, not just IR and recovery. For publicly-traded manufacturers and their suppliers, an OT-impacting incident that halts production can be material, so legal, finance and security need a pre-agreed process to assess materiality and disclose on a tight timeline — before the incident forces the question.
